summary: Conchiglie with Swiss chard and smoked mozzarella plus the author's rules for a great American "kitchen sink" pasta: shaped pasta, aggressively salted water (1.5 tablespoons per gallon), a big-flavor ingredient, a crunchy garnish, and a minute of tossing with reserved pasta water; serves 3-4 as a main.
glance: 1 pound conchiglie, pulled just barely al dente; reserve 1 cup pasta water
chard, artichoke bottoms, white beans, 1/2 cup dry sherry and 2/3 pound cubed smoked mozzarella
1/4 cup lightly toasted green pumpkin seeds as a final garnish
Vegetarian; not vegan or gluten-free but adaptable
faq: Use shaped pasta rather than strands for chunky sauces; salt the water aggressively (1.5 tablespoons per gallon) at a rolling boil and pull the pasta when al dente; choose at least one big-flavor ingredient and one crunchy ingredient (used as a final garnish so it doesn't get soggy); aim for a range of sweet, salty, bitter, sour, herbaceous, umami and spicy flavors.

The author says what he's seen in Italy favors simple pastas with just a few components, often as a prelude to a heartier second course. This style is more of an American take, with a thoughtfully chosen kitchen sink of ingredients, interesting enough to be a meal on its own.
What if I'm short on fresh ingredients?
Open the pantry or freezer for roasted red peppers, olives, capers, frozen baby peas and the like.
Why toss the pasta with the sauce and pasta water?

Toss the cooked pasta with the sauce for a minute over a moderate flame so the flavors marry, adding the reserved water as needed to loosen it. The water is salted and slightly thick from starch, so it moistens without diluting flavors.
What makes up the sauce in this version?

There's no real sauce beyond the melting smoked mozzarella and a little sherry: garlic, onion, thyme, sage and chili flakes, chard cooked covered, artichoke bottoms, white beans and sherry, scraped up with the pan's caramelized flavors.
